```{python}
# define map layout function
def apply_map_layout_and_controls(fig, title_text, years):
    """
    Applies the carto-positron map style, playback menus, and time sliders
    to an existing Plotly animation figure.
    """
    fig.update_layout(
        title=title_text,
        map=dict(
            style="carto-positron",
            center=dict(lat=37.8, lon=-96),
            zoom=3
        ),
        margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=50, b=0),
        updatemenus=[
            dict(
                type="buttons",
                showactive=False,
                x=0.05,
                y=0.95,
                buttons=[
                    dict(
                        label="Play",
                        method="animate",
                        args=[None, {"frame": {"duration": 700, "redraw": True}, "transition": {"duration": 300}, "fromcurrent": True}]
                    ),
                    dict(
                        label="Pause",
                        method="animate",
                        args=[[None], {"frame": {"duration": 0, "redraw": False}, "transition": {"duration": 0}, "mode": "immediate"}]
                    )
                ]
            )
        ],
        sliders=[
            dict(
                active=0,
                currentvalue={"prefix": "Year: "},
                pad={"t": 30},
                steps=[
                    dict(
                        label=str(int(y)),
                        method="animate",
                        args=[[str(int(y))], {"frame": {"duration": 0, "redraw": True}, "transition": {"duration": 0}, "mode": "immediate"}]
                    )
                    for y in years
                ]
            )
        ]
    )
    return fig
```


#### Missingness Check
```{python}
# create map of counties for which we have data over time
def plot_county_coverage(df, table_name, value_col):
    map_df = df[["year", "county_id"]].dropna().drop_duplicates()
    years = sorted(map_df["year"].unique())
    frames = []

    # Compile chronological frame tracking data
    for year in years:
        df_year = map_df[map_df["year"] == year]
        frames.append(
            go.Frame(
                data=[
                    go.Choroplethmap(
                        locations=df_year["county_id"],
                        z=[1] * len(df_year),  
                    )
                ],
                name=str(int(year))
            )
        )

    if not frames:
        raise ValueError(f"No valid yearly data found for {table_name}")

    # Create base map matching geojson object
    initial_year_data = map_df[map_df["year"] == years[0]]
    fig = go.Figure(
        data=[
            go.Choroplethmap(
                geojson=counties_geojson, # References global object directly
                locations=initial_year_data["county_id"],
                z=[1] * len(initial_year_data),
                featureidkey="id",
                colorscale=[[0, "#fff9f9"], [1, "#2cb94f"]],
                zmin=0,
                zmax=1,
                marker_opacity=0.35,
                marker_line_width=0.3,
                showscale=False,
                hovertemplate="County FIPS: %{location}<br>Has data: Yes<extra></extra>"
            )
        ],
        frames=frames
    )
        
    # Map styling and playback controls
    title_text = f"{table_name}: {value_col} by county and year"
    fig = apply_map_layout_and_controls(fig, title_text, years)

    return fig

plot_county_coverage(df, "Unemployment", "county coverage")
```



#### Values by County

```{python}
# create a choropleth map of counties for a set of desired variables in the df

# Update these:
eda_table_name = "Unemployment"
cols_to_use = [1,2,3,4]

## one map per column
for i in cols_to_use:
    value_col = cols[i]
    map_df = df[["year", "county_id", value_col]].dropna()

    ## Get unique years
    years = sorted(map_df["year"].dropna().unique())

    frames = []

    value_min = map_df[value_col].min()
    value_max = map_df[value_col].max()


    frames = []
    for year in years:
        df_year = map_df[map_df["year"] == year] # dropped .copy() for speed
        
        frames.append(
            go.Frame(
                data=[
                    go.Choroplethmap(
                        locations=df_year["county_id"],
                        z=df_year[value_col]
                    )
                ],
                name=str(int(year))
            )
        )

    if not frames:
        raise ValueError(f"No valid yearly data found for {value_col}")

    initial_year_df = map_df[map_df["year"] == years[0]]

    fig = go.Figure(
        data=[
            go.Choroplethmap(
                geojson=counties_geojson, 
                locations=initial_year_df["county_id"],
                z=initial_year_df[value_col],
                featureidkey="id",
                colorscale="Viridis",
                zmin=value_min,
                zmax=value_max,
                marker_opacity=0.5,
                marker_line_width=0.3,
                colorbar=dict(title=value_col),
                hovertemplate=f"County FIPS: %{{location}}<br>{value_col}: %{{z}}<extra></extra>"
            )
        ],
        frames=frames
    )
        
    ## Make it look nice
    title_text = f"{eda_table_name}: {value_col} by county and year"
    fig = apply_map_layout_and_controls(fig, title_text, years)

    fig.show()
```

## Summary of Findings

- There are no NA values for any of the columns in this dataset
- The ranges for all value columns are quite high
- The standard deviations of civilian labor force, employed, and unemployed are all more than double the means
- There are no 0 values for any columns in the dataset
- The distributions of all value columns are heavily right-skewed (except for unemployment rate, which is only moderately right-skewed)
- After using a logarithmic scale, civilian labor force, employed, and unemployed are actually extremely normally distributed
- There appears to be high correlation between civilian labor force, employed, and unemployed
- Unemployment rate appears to be only positively correlated with unemployed
- Notably there are missing counties in a few places:
    - One county in SD, which looks like it may be on a reservation
    - A few counties in Virginia, mostly very small but one large one in Norfolk
    - **The ENTIRE state of Louisiana**
- The maps for civilian labor force, employed, and unemployed all look fairly uniform, with large population centers being more lightly colored (higher number)
- The map for unemployment rate is more varied, with some clear geographical trends, such as the middle of the country generally having lower unemployment rates.
